newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil millers ask govt to allow U.S wheat imports.
newsitem.headline: Brazil millers ask govt to allow U.S wheat imports.

text.p: The Brazilian Wheat Industries Association (Abitrigo) has asked the government to renew a waiver on phytosanitary conditions for U.S. wheat which would allow immediate imports into Brazil, Abitrigo's head said.
"The government should give me a reply tomorrow," said Antenor Barros Leal.
But an official at the Agriculture Ministry's plant inspections department said he had not heard of any likely change in Brazilian policy with regard to U.S. wheat imports.

Brazilian and U.S. officials have been negotiating over stricter Brazilian entry requirements for wheat which in theory took effect as of January 1 last year but which only came into practice after a waiver expired at the end of September 1996.
The problems center on the tilletia controversa kuhn, or TCK fungus, which has been found only in very limited areas in northern U.S. states, government officials said.
But because U.S. inspectors do not normally know the origin of the wheat, they are unable to guarantee "free of TCK" on a federal certificate as is necessary under the new rules.
The Brazilian government has suggested sending Brazilian inspectors to the U.S. to take samples of any wheat before it is shipped but this, traders say, is impractical.
The issue is expected to be discussed at two international technical meetings on plant diseases, first in Washington next month and then in Brazil in October, the Agriculture Ministry official said.
"At the meeting in Brazil, we want to define once and for all if the conditions exist in Brazil for TCK," he said.
"I think by next year, the whole issue should be resolved," he added.
The U.S. had not been expected to export much wheat to Brazil this year because of a bumper Argentine harvest.

But Abitrigo's current push to renew the phytosanitary waiver for U.S. imports is because of supply shortages caused by recent weather disruptions in shipments from the Argentine port of Necochea, Leal said.
Leal estimated that around 500,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat would be needed to be brought in.
However other millers said that even if the government did renew the waiver, it was already too late to bring in U.S. wheat given the domestic harvest is due to start next month.
